raw_text:
# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: Current Evidence, Clinical Practice, and Future Horizons

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major driver of ischemic stroke, with the left atrial appendage (LAA) serving as the anatomical source of thrombi in over 90% of non-valvular AF cases [1]. While oral anticoagulants (OACs), including direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), remain the standard of care for stroke prevention, their long-term use is frequently limited by bleeding events, patient non-compliance, and absolute contraindications. Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as a validated, non-pharmacological alternative for patients seeking stroke protection without the burden of lifelong anticoagulation.

### Clinical Trial Evidence

The landmark PROTECT AF [2] and PREVAIL [3] randomized clinical trials established the non-inferiority of the first-generation WATCHMAN device compared to warfarin. Initial short-term data were reinforced by longer-term follow-up at 2.3 years [4] and 4 years [5], culminating in a pooled 5-year patient-level meta-analysis [6]. These studies demonstrated that LAAC not only offers comparable stroke prevention to warfarin but also significantly reduces major bleeding, hemorrhagic stroke, and cardiovascular mortality. Real-world registries such as EWOLUTION [7] and multicenter experiences with the Amplatzer Cardiac Plug [8] confirmed these safety and efficacy profiles in unselected, high-risk patient populations.

More recently, the PRAGUE-17 trial compared LAAC directly with DOACs (primarily apixaban) in patients at high risk for both thromboembolic and bleeding events [9]. At 4 years of follow-up, PRAGUE-17 confirmed that LAAC was non-inferior to DOACs for the composite endpoint of stroke, cardiovascular death, or major bleeding, providing compelling evidence for its utility in direct comparison to modern pharmacotherapy [10].

### Device Innovations and Comparative Trials

Device technology has evolved to optimize closure, simplify implantation, and minimize procedural complications. The introduction of the WATCHMAN FLX device, evaluated in the PINNACLE FLX trial [11], improved upon its predecessor with a fully recapturable, closed-end design that reduces the risk of embolization and peridevice leaks. Real-world registries, including the SURPASS study, have validated the high procedural success rate and low complication rates of this next-generation device [12].

Concurrently, the Amplatzer Amulet device, which features a disc-and-lobe design, was evaluated in a large global observational study [13] and directly compared to the first-generation WATCHMAN in the landmark Amulet IDE trial [14]. Amulet was found to be non-inferior for stroke prevention and superior in achieving complete LAA closure, though it carried a slightly higher rate of early peri-procedural complications [14].

### Technical Aspects and Imaging

Successful LAAC depends heavily on precise pre-procedural planning and intra-procedural imaging. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and, increasingly, intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) are utilized to guide transseptal puncture, assess LAA anatomy, size the device, and confirm stable positioning [15]. High-resolution imaging is crucial for minimizing residual peridevice leaks (PDL) [16]. While small leaks (<5 mm) were historically considered benign, recent registry data suggest that even minor residual flow can increase the risk of long-term thromboembolic events [16].

### Post-Procedural Management and Complications

Optimal post-procedural antithrombotic therapy remains a subject of ongoing investigation [17, 18]. Standard regimens historically transitioned from temporary OAC and aspirin to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), and eventually single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT). For patients with absolute contraindications to OAC, the ASAP study demonstrated that a DAPT-only post-implantation regimen is safe and feasible [19].

A key clinical challenge is device-related thrombus (DRT), which occurs in approximately 2% to 4% of patients [20, 21, 22]. DRT is associated with an increased risk of stroke and systemic embolism, requiring prompt treatment with temporary anticoagulation [21].

### Guidelines and Special Populations

Current guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [23] and the joint ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS [24] provide a Class IIb recommendation for LAAC in patients with AF who have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation. Expert consensus statements support its use in carefully selected patients [25]. 

Specifically, observational data have shown substantial clinical benefit in ultra-high-risk patients, such as those with prior intracranial hemorrhage, where LAAC significantly reduces bleeding without compromising stroke prevention [26, 27, 28]. Meta-analyses and large-scale registry comparisons continue to support LAAC as a durable, cost-effective, and safe alternative to long-term OAC [29, 30].
